questions.text: An array [latex][82,101,90,11,111,75,33,131,44,93] [/latex] is heapified. Which one of the following options represents the first three elements in the heapified array?
questions.solution:
Build a max-heap bottom-up (heapify from index [latex]\lfloor10/2\rfloor=5[/latex] down to 1):
[82, 101, 90, 11, 111, 75, 33, 131, 44, 93]

- i=5 (111): child 93 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] no change.
- i=4 (11): children 131, 44 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] swap with 131.
- i=3 (90): children 75, 33 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] no change.
- i=2 (101): children 131, 111 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] swap with 131 (101 then fine above 11, 44).
- i=1 (82): swap with 131, then with 111, then with 93.

Heap: [131, 111, 90, 101, 93, 75, 33, 11, 44, 82]

Answer: 131, 111, 90

questions.text:
Consider the following recurrence relation:
[latex] T(n)=\left\{\begin{array}{c} \sqrt{n} T(\sqrt{n})+n \text { for } n \geq 1, \\ 1 \quad \text { for } n=1 . \end{array}\right. [/latex]
Which one of the following options is CORRECT?
questions.solution:
Divide both sides by [latex]n[/latex]: [latex]\frac{T(n)}{n}=\frac{T(\sqrt n)}{\sqrt n}+1[/latex].

Let [latex]S(n)=\frac{T(n)}{n}[/latex]. Then [latex]S(n)=S(\sqrt n)+1[/latex].

Taking square roots repeatedly, [latex]n\to n^{1/2}\to n^{1/4}\to\cdots[/latex] reaches a constant after [latex]\log\log n[/latex] steps, adding 1 each step. So [latex]S(n)=\Theta(\log\log n)[/latex].

[latex]T(n)=n\,S(n)=\Theta(n\log\log n)[/latex]

Answer: [latex]T(n)=\Theta(n\log\log n)[/latex]

questions.text: Consider a binary min-heap containing 105 distinct elements. Let [latex]k[/latex]  be the index (in the underlying array) of the maximum element stored in the heap. The number of possible values of [latex]k[/latex] is
questions.solution:
In a min-heap every parent is smaller than its children, so the maximum element cannot have a child [latex]\text{---}[/latex] it must be a leaf. Any leaf can hold it.

In an array heap of [latex]n[/latex] elements, leaves are at indices [latex]\lfloor n/2\rfloor+1[/latex] to [latex]n[/latex].

[latex]n=105[/latex]: leaves are 53 to 105 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] [latex]105-52=53[/latex] positions.

Answer: 53

questions.text: The symbol [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] indicates functional dependency in the context of a relational database. Which of the following options is/are TRUE?
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- [latex](X,Y)\rightarrow(Z,W)[/latex] does not give [latex]X\rightarrow(Z,W)[/latex]; Y may be required [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.
- Decomposition rule: [latex]XY\rightarrow ZW[/latex] [latex]\Rightarrow[/latex] [latex]XY\rightarrow Z[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- Pseudo-transitivity: [latex]W\rightarrow Y[/latex] [latex]\Rightarrow[/latex] [latex]XW\rightarrow XY[/latex] (augment by X), and [latex]XY\rightarrow Z[/latex], so [latex]XW\rightarrow Z[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- Transitivity: [latex]X\rightarrow Y,\;Y\rightarrow Z[/latex] [latex]\Rightarrow[/latex] [latex]X\rightarrow Z[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.

Answer: Options 2, 3 and 4

[latex] (X \rightarrow Y \text { and } Y \rightarrow Z) \text { implies } X \rightarrow Z [/latex]

questions.text: Let [latex] G [/latex] be a directed graph and [latex] T [/latex] a depth first search (DFS) spanning tree in [latex] G [/latex] that is rooted at a vertex [latex] v [/latex]. Suppose [latex] T [/latex] is also a breadth first search (BFS) tree in [latex] G [/latex], rooted at [latex] v [/latex]. Which of the following statements is/are TRUE for every such graph [latex] G [/latex] and tree [latex] T [/latex] ?
questions.solution:
In a BFS tree, every edge [latex]u\rightarrow w[/latex] of G satisfies [latex]level(w)\le level(u)+1[/latex].

A forward edge goes from [latex]u[/latex] to a non-child descendant [latex]w[/latex], so [latex]level(w)\ge level(u)+2[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] this contradicts BFS. Hence there are no forward edges [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.

The others can fail:
- Back edge: G = {v[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]a, a[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]v}. Tree {v[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]a} is both DFS and BFS tree; a[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]v is a back edge.
- Cross edge: G = {v[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]a, v[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]b, b[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]a}. DFS visits a then b; b[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]a is a cross edge, and the tree is also the BFS tree.
- So G can also have edges outside T.

Answer: There are no forward-edges in G with respect to T

There are no cross-edges in [latex] G [/latex] with respect to the tree [latex] T [/latex]
There are no forward-edges in [latex] G [/latex] with respect to the tree [latex] T [/latex]
The only edges in [latex] G [/latex] are the edges in [latex] T [/latex]
